slug: 2023-12-07-zhangxiaojun-95后创业者把马斯克值拉满-但偶像其实是毛主席
title: Post-95 founders max out their Musk score, but their idol is actually Mao Zedong
dek: What drives this wave of young founders isn't money, it's ‘if this thing is badass, just build it first’; they don't write BPs, don't chase leaderboards, don't do PR proactively, and only accumulate reputation within the circles they care about.
why: A 1997-born founder gives his first interview, laying out clearly the real differences between this new generation of founders and the previous one in drive, idols, and management style, with concrete details.
who: Founders and investors watching AI startups, AIGC applications, and 3D generation, plus anyone who wants to understand the real state of post-95 and post-00 founders.
skip: The personal history section from 2:13 to 8:02 can be fast-forwarded; information density is low.

points.h: AI 1.0 was parameter tuning, 2.0 is general models
points.body: Song Yacheng draws the difference between SenseTime and Minimax very clearly: the AI 1.0 era was a large number of scientists using manual parameter tuning to solve long-tail problems one by one — face recognition, OCR, vehicle recognition, illegal dumping, one algorithm per scenario. By AI 2.0, it's the brute-force aesthetics of data driven, using one general large model to solve general problems, then growing niche applications on top of the model. His judgment is ‘it's a very black-box thing’ — not covering the long tail with small algorithms plus technical architecture, but optimizing a very general model.

points.h: Half a year without salaries, 30-plus people held on
points.body: They started the company at the end of last year, right when the US was raising rates, Russia and Ukraine were at war, and everything that should have blown up and shouldn't have blown up all blew up. Asking FAs, they all said VCs might barely invest in 2023. Song Yacheng put in his own money, and the company only officially started paying salaries in June; before that, for half a year, no one had been paid. The team of about thirty-plus people kept going. He says this is a characteristic of post-95 and post-00 founders — ‘we are a group of people with a lot of faith’.

points.h: The Musk score is demanding that essential thing to death
points.body: Song Yacheng's definition of ‘Musk score’: knowing very clearly what I want, then I want these one, two, three, and no matter what method I will achieve them; if someone comes who can help me achieve it, then achieve it, if not, replace them. His example is going to SIGGRAPH this August to give a Keynote — the top graphics conference's fiftieth anniversary, fifty or sixty thousand attendees, with Nvidia's Jensen Huang, IBM, Unity, Sony each speaking for an hour, and them too. Never in history had a Chinese person given a Keynote at SIGGRAPH. The organizing committee at one point suspected they were a shell company; they asked partners like Blender's CEO to write recommendation letters proving the company really existed, went through two or three rounds of interviews, and in the end what he went to talk about was ‘I'm actually not here to talk about technology’.

points.h: 3D data is scarce, they scraped together 11 million entries
points.body: He breaks AI into three things: the horse trainer (algorithm), the racetrack (compute), and the fodder (data). 3D is an extremely data-scarce field — most people have written Weibo, posted to Moments, shot videos, but never K'd a 3D model. At the time, OpenAI's private dataset was 2 million, Nvidia's 1 million, other big companies about 700,000. As a startup, they spent a lot of time working with games, animation, film and TV, model communities, and databases, wearing them down and showing their faces, and finally got 11 million high-quality data entries — 3D native data hand-K'd one by one by people in games, animation, and film. A single model costing tens or hundreds of dollars is normal; buying is unaffordable.

points.h: His startup idol is Mao Zedong, not Musk
points.body: Song Yacheng says most people around him answer Elon Musk first when asked about startup idols, but he's a bit different — his idol is Mao Zedong. The reason is he cares a lot about faith: the soul of a company lies in having faith, and things done with faith don't need to be told to him every day, he'll do them himself. He observes that most post-80 founders didn't go abroad in middle school but went abroad for a master's, and their idols are generally people like Jobs; while his generation went out earlier, and their idols are different. He distinguishes Jobs and Musk: Jobs is pulling an MP4 out of your pocket since childhood, Musk does sci-fi experiences, ‘dragging nine bars faster than nine bars’.

points.h: Two completely opposite kinds of people live in an AIGC company
points.body: The technical people are relatively rational, more I-type, a bit socially anxious, don't like team building, each managing a module like an assembly line, with extremely high degrees — they now have nearly 20 PhDs, basically all Tsinghua bachelor's, master's, and PhDs. The product people need a very warm culture: eating together, chatting about games and animation, going to CP conventions and ChinaJoy, playing games and watching anime during work hours, a cozy office environment. The two groups have different social tokens and values: one thinks what's badass is games that have made money, products with high DAU; the other thinks what's badass is 50 papers, 40,000 citations. How to bring these two cultures together is a problem many AIGC companies need to solve.

points.h: Old hands paired with young geniuses, a deliberate team-building method
points.body: Song Yacheng says he did this subconsciously: every team is ‘a very experienced startup old hand who has done zero-to-one successfully’ paired with ‘a very aspiring, young, highly execution-oriented genius who wants to prove themselves’. Technical CTO Liang Ding was SenseTime's general model lead, an early SenseTime employee, led hundreds of people, spent nine years at SenseTime; chief scientist Cao Yanpei previously founded a 3D startup acquired by Kuaishou, then led 3D generation at Tencent. Most technical people are post-95, including Guo Wencheng, founder of 3D Stable Diffusion, born in 1997. He uses finding an oasis as an analogy: old hands can smell it, know how much supplies to bring and how to distribute them; geniuses might ride a bicycle into the desert and are more likely to discover new things.

points.h: Abundant capital is a curse, the trough forces productization
points.body: Song Yacheng says he's very glad to be starting a company at this time. When the capital environment is especially good, companies easily raise a lot of money, so there's no urgency to ship products or actually make money, and no focus; there are lots of resources to waste, and in the end maybe three to five years pass with no product, no substantial money made, and the company is gone — he calls this ‘the curse of startup resources’. Instead, companies that come out of a capital market trough think from day one about how to productize, how to commercialize; the optimization target is user experience, and what each person manages is the user's expectations, not the boss's expectations. He says the sense of crisis at the end of 2022 and early 2023 made him clearer, turning him back from the mental circuit of ‘startup means fundraising’.

points.h: GPT isn't as fast as imagined, and fundraising methods changed too
points.body: He analyzes two key points in the worsening fundraising environment in the second half of this year: first, China-US relations, some mainstream dollar institutions encountering difficulties; second, OpenAI and GPT haven't developed as fast as people imagined. When ChatGPT first came out, everyone off the top of their heads thought AGI would be achieved immediately, AIGC could generate everything, and it would overturn the world in a year or two. But by this year GPT is still GPT4, AIGC can only replace 30% of art, and the maturity of Runway and 3D generation is still insufficient. The gap makes investors conservative. The response is to change the fundraising rhythm: no longer waiting three months to close round by round, but if there's 100 million you can talk, directly invest a round in, short, fast, and flexible.

points.h: Miaoya and Heizhen are templates, 3D lacks a content platform
points.body: Song Yacheng thinks AIGC has found quite a few paradigms this year: Miaoya stipulates you can only shoot yourself, only ID photos, it's a template; Heizhen can make Guo Degang speak English, make Musk speak Chinese, also a content template. But these may be flash-in-the-pan phenomenon products, because there's no content platform to take on the traffic and creators. He judges the biggest opportunity is in 3D — because 3D has no content platform. If you go do a video content platform, TikTok already exists, and squeezing it is very hard; but 3D is a relatively blue ocean, with space to create a 3D content platform.

I just want data, I don't care what good thing, I just want data, and this data must be at least one quantum more than others.
What Jobs made is a product experience that makes people feel great, comfortable, high-end. What Elon Musk makes is a sci-fi experience.
The biggest barrier is time, it's that in your life, you put time...
Instead, we see that those great companies all come from the trough of the capital market.
You might as well be from day one a very muscular muscle man, but he has no fat, and he only throws one punch, just this one punch is enough.
Their, or our, management method is faith, I think this is a very important thing, only if you have enough faith, enough love...
